output.headline: Climate campaigners inch toward a win as Rosebank oilfield decision nears
output.bodyHtml:
Miatta Fahnbulleh is minded to reject the giant Rosebank oilfield, sources have told the Guardian, in what would be a major victory for climate campaigners and a real setback for the North Sea energy industry.

After approving the smaller Jackdaw gasfield on Wednesday, officials say the energy secretary is leaning towards refusing approval for what would be one of the biggest oilfields in the North Sea.

But she could still be overruled by Andy Burnham, who may hear different representations from the chancellor, John Healey. A final decision is expected before the end of this year.

In comments that will be read as a signal of her intent, Fahnbulleh told the Guardian that the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it.

“One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.”

Healey, in contrast, told ITV he expected “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, a suggestion he is anticipating new oil revenues. Burnham would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision.

Fahnbulleh has promised that future revenues from the North Sea will be spent on green energy projects through a new energy wealth fund. She said the fund would be given £2bn in the budget.

“When we have tax revenues that are coming from the oil and gas industry, it is right that we invest that in the transition we need to make in energy,” she said, adding that the money would be spent on renewables, nuclear and other clean energy schemes.

However, she could not say exactly which tax revenues would be given to the new fund, or how much that might generate. “The chancellor will make those details clear in the budget,” she said.

Labour MPs warned on Wednesday there would be a major pushback in the party if Rosebank was approved, though most are prepared to accept the arguments that Jackdaw was a necessity as part of the transition to net zero.

MPs are understood to have discussed ways of forcing or encouraging a parliamentary vote on Rosebank should it be approved, as a way of expressing dissent.

Officials say Fahnbulleh has not yet taken a final decision on Rosebank. The field would emit about seven times the carbon of Jackdaw and Fahnbulleh is understood to believe that it would do less for UK energy security, given most of the oil would be exported.

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “This is speculation. As the energy secretary has said, each project will be assessed on its own merits.”

On a visit to Aberdeen, Fahnbulleh said she had been satisfied that Jackdaw, which is due to begin producing gas within weeks and will add an estimated 36m tonnes of carbon emissions, would not violate the UK’s climate commitments.

“As we make the transition, we are going to need gas,” she said. “At a point when we have got conflict in the Middle East that is triggering an energy crisis, energy security is vital, and homegrown energy is key.”

She said, however, it would not help achieve the government’s main energy target of bringing down bills, saying: “This is not about bills.”

The UN Environment Programme has recommended that global carbon emissions be cut by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin.

The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted.

But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.

One Labour MP close to the energy secretary said she knew her credibility was “on the line” and that she was able to show she was pragmatic by approving Jackdaw but drawing the line at Rosebank. “She’s putting up a fight and I want to be supportive of Miatta – I understand what she is fighting,” they said.

But they said the decision would ultimately come down to Burnham. “Andy is not a climate guy – he is under pressure. If he wants to do it, he’ll do it.”

Several serving ministers have said they would find Rosebank a more difficult decision to back and it would cause greater problems in their constituencies.

The former minister Catherine West said climate change “is not a future threat but a present reality” and that the answer to job losses in the North Sea was not to “double down on new fossil fuel developments”.

Afzal Khan, the Labour MP for Manchester Rusholme and chair of the all-party parliamentary group on climate change, said: “Approving projects on the scale of Rosebank, on top of today’s decision to approve Jackdaw, cannot be justified.”

Burnham is seeking more ways to lower energy bills, telling MPs on Wednesday that ministers would consider whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills to ease cost pressures on households.

While Labour’s 2024 election manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, the companies behind Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfield project have sought approval for existing licences.

The Greens said on Wednesday they intended to fight seats directly on the issue of Jackdaw and Rosebank. The Green MP Carla Denyer said: “We have identified dozens of seats where we are Labour’s main challenger and the climate is one of the top issues and voters have been mobilised by the heatwave and wildfires.

“Our strong advice to Labour MPs is to stand up to Andy Burnham and his act of climate violence, both to save your seats and, far more importantly, to protect the planet for future generations.”
output.standfirst: Exclusive: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh is minded not to approve the oilfield, a win for climate campaigners but a real setback for the North Sea energy industry; the decision is not final and follows this week's approval of the smaller Jackdaw gasfield.
output.progress: Fahnbulleh is weighing Rosebank against the UK's climate commitments, and plans a new fund putting future oil and gas revenue into renewables and nuclear power.

output.headline: MPs press MoD for 'dramatic progress' on submarines and warships by 2030
output.bodyHtml:
Britain risks failing to deter future Russian aggression in the high north beyond the UK because of shortfalls in the number and availability of Royal Navy submarines and warships, MPs on the defence select committee have said.

The committee focused on the slow deployment of HMS Dragon to Cyprus this spring, declining numbers of frigates, and reports that all five Astute-class attack submarines were in dock this summer as evidence of a navy under-resourced for the threat.

“The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the high north,” said Tan Dhesi, the committee chair. “Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments.”

The high north, the seas beyond Scotland, have become increasingly strategically significant amid growing Russian interest in energy pipelines and undersea cables at a time when Arctic seaways are opening up because of global heating.

The navy shadowed a Russian spy ship, the Yantar, operating inside the UK’s economic waters in November and January last year, accusing sailors onboard of trying to map strategic cables and shining lasers at RAF pilots monitoring them.

Russia also wants to assert control over the emerging northern sea route, a 3,500-mile (5,600km) shipping lane running along the country’s Arctic coast. It is the quickest maritime route from China to Europe, navigable last year for four and half months.

The MPs argued the UK needed to make “dramatic progress” before the end of the decade, and they called on the Ministry of Defence to draw up a plan to ensure more warships and submarines are at sea by 2030.

The problem would be particularly acute, the committee added, if the US did not support the UK in a crisis, a rare cross-party acknowledgment that under Donald Trump, US military help cannot be relied on, particularly if a small Nato member in the region was threatened or attacked.

“There would be critical military gaps if the United States were not involved in countering such [Russian] aggression,” the MPs said, and they argued that the UK, as the next largest Nato military in the region, had to be prepared to increase its navy.

It took more than three weeks for HMS Dragon, a destroyer, to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean in March after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone. No warships were available and Dragon had to be hauled out of dry dock to deploy.

The navy has five frigates with sonar dedicated to detecting Russian submarines at distance, the committee noted, lower than a target of eight, as ageing warships have been scrapped without replacements coming into service. It could take until 2037 before it reaches its stated requirement, the committee added.

None of Britain’s five Astute submarines, also used to track Russian maritime activity, were at sea from June and into the summer. They were in dock for a mixture of short-term and long-term refits, the committee noted, and they also lack the capability to operate under ice, unlike their Russian equivalents, although certification exercises are in progress.

However, no significant extra money is expected to be available for defence until the next decade, with Andy Burnham’s government committed to medium-term spending plans agreed under Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer.

Though Starmer agreed to lift defence spending by about £30bn a year to 3.5% of GDP in 2035, he would only sign off spending to the lower level of 2.7% by 2030. That prompted the resignation of John Healey as defence secretary, only for him to return as chancellor under Burnham, with the old spending plans intact.

In response to the report, an MoD spokesperson highlighted a recent £330m investment to protect undersea infrastructure, and noted that Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, had visited Iceland this month and watched how HMS St Albans, a frigate, tracked Russian submarines in the north Atlantic. “We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses,” they added.
output.standfirst: The Ministry of Defence points to a £330m investment in undersea infrastructure and a Royal Navy frigate tracking Russian submarines near Iceland, after a defence committee said the Navy faces shortfalls in submarines and warships and must make 'dramatic progress' within the decade.
output.progress: The MoD highlights a £330m investment in undersea infrastructure and points to a Royal Navy frigate tracking Russian submarines during a recent ministerial visit to Iceland.

output.headline: Researchers use AI to expose decades-old flaw in PHP, used by 70% of sites
output.bodyHtml:
The organisation behind PHP issued a patch on Wednesday after researchers testing cyberdefences discovered a serious vulnerability in the computer language, used to build much of the world wide web.

The US National Security Agency told all organisations using PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately. It said the vulnerability could “provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database”.

OpenAI said it led a coalition of researchers that discovered the flaw and claimed “frontier AI” had been key. The researcher who found the weakness, however, said they used models available to the public.

Cybersecurity company Calif said in a blog post it found the flaws with the help of a large language model on 1 August and had been working on a fix ever since. Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post that it too had discovered it with the help of Wiz Atlas, its autonomous AI vulnerability research tool, as well as Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.

Websites around the globe went dark as a precaution while the fix was rolled out.

Belgian, Dutch, Finnish, French and German sites were among those that governments took down temporarily as they scrambled to patch the critical weakness in PHP, a language used by almost 70% of websites.

The vulnerability in the programming language, which became public on Tuesday, sparked warnings from national security agencies in Washington and London. It means millions of websites will need to be fixed. One internet infrastructure expert said Russian state actors or organised criminals could exploit the flaw to carry out cyber-attacks.

Related: What is PHP, and how bad is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns globally?

Wordpress, one of the most common website systems, uses PHP, as does Wikipedia, the messaging software Slack and – at least historically – much of Facebook. The Wikimedia Foundation said it had taken down several systems on Wednesday as a precautionary measure until they could be patched.

The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for “backdoors installed by an attacker”.

Because a fix is now public and AI tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers ⁠jumped to get ahead of the updates.

AI was powering a “race to exploit”, said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the “mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet”.

Prof Alan Woodward, a cybersecurity expert at Surrey University, said: “It was very surprising and troubling because of the extent to which PHP was used around the world. PHP issued a patch very quickly. The big thing is for everyone using it to get that in to make sure their systems are safe.

“The troubling part is there is going to be a long tail of websites who may not be maintained as well and they are going to remain vulnerable, which means we may see weeks and months of ongoing attacks. For the big juicy targets, I hope to goodness they are being patched quickly.”

Related: World leaders must wise up to threat of cyber-attacks or rogue fridges will be least of their worries | Heather Stewart

Woodward said there was a window of opportunity for bad actors. “There is this race and some people unfortunately don’t even know they are in the race.”

The vulnerabilities remained hidden ‌in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to take advantage of, Wiz’s post said.

In a blog post late on Wednesday, Amazon security chief CJ Moses said its security team detected an attempt to exploit the vulnerabilities against one of its decoy “honeypot” systems on 17 October, four days before public disclosure.

The attempt on the system came from an anonymous internet address, suggesting the activity was conducted by a threat actor, Moses said, adding that it was unclear how the actor learned of the flaws while they were under embargo.

In a statement, the ​White House said it was made aware of the flaw on Friday.

In the UK, websites belonging to Edinburgh, Bristol and Oxford councils were taken offline. In France, local government websites including that of the Paris police prefecture went offline on Wednesday, as did in the Netherlands the national digital identity service, the website of the house of representatives and the site of the national cybersecurity centre.

The Australian Signals Directorate was temporarily affected by the outage overnight local time, with the national cyber defence agency noting other government websites may have been similarly affected.

Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert, said: “There’s going to be a lot of automatic exploitation of this.” The bug might allow cryptocurrency miners to exploit vulnerable servers at other people’s expense, he said.

He also said large crime organisations and Russian state actors could use the vulnerable sites as a launching pad from which to conduct distributed denial of service (DDoS) and other cyber-attacks.

The issue highlighted the poor state of internet infrastructure, Woźniak said, something that was being brought to light by advancing AI models but that had been a long-developing problem. The underlying vulnerabilities the researcher found were decades old.

“This is an environmental problem in an industry where there’s an incentive to move fast and make changes,” he said. “There’s an incentive to deploy a thing and then never update it and not think about maintenance.”
output.standfirst: Sites worldwide, including government services, went offline as a precaution while PHP's maintainers rolled out a fix for the decades-old flaw, which AI tools helped researchers discover in code used by 70% of websites; experts say hackers could still exploit it before patching completes.
output.progress: The organisation behind PHP issued a patch within a day of disclosure, and the NSA and NCSC gave guidance on checking for intrusions.

output.headline: Aneurin Bevan emerges vindicated as his MI5 file proves 'remarkably tame'
output.bodyHtml:
Aneurin “Nye” Bevan, the Welsh Labour firebrand who spearheaded the creation of the NHS, had a personal file that was “remarkably tame”, according to official papers now released to the public, despite being monitored by security services for more than two decades.

Although there is nothing in the files to indicate that MI5 ever tapped Bevan’s phone or intercepted his mail, one officer wrote in 1943: “I do not think that Bevan’s activities are a matter in which we, the Security Service, should be involved. In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently, as any copy of Hansard will show, and it would not therefore be possible to do anything positive.” Reviewing the file again after Bevan’s death in 1960, another MI5 officer agreed: “Considering what a controversial character Nye Bevan was, the file is remarkably tame.”

Papers released to the National Archives show Bevan came to MI5’s attention in the 1930s over concerns about his links with known communists, and that monitoring continued even after he became a minister in the postwar Labour government that created the NHS. MI5 first opened a personal file on the then backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale, in south Wales, in 1933, describing him as having “inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the communist cause.”

He was also noted to have been “in close touch” with Harry Pollitt, general secretary of the Communist party of Great Britain, and others in the party who backed his plan to organise “workers’ freedom groups” to defend against “capitalists”.

Bevan fell out with his communist allies, who complained he was not interested in workers’ unity and was intent on building “a movement of his own” – but by 1936 they had reconciled, with Bevan supporting an application by the Communist party to affiliate with the Labour party.

In 1949, MI5 became concerned about Bevan’s friendship with Wilfred Macartney, who had been convicted of spying for Russia in 1928. Recordings of Macartney’s conversations suggested he was passing on information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt, which led the director general, Sir Percy Sillitoe, to approach the prime minister, Clement Attlee, to warn him. Attlee dismissed Macartney’s claims as a “tissue of lies” but agreed to “warn” Bevan about Macartney.

The file was finally closed in 1975, 15 years after Bevan died.

Other newly released papers show MI5 feared communists could attempt to disrupt the coronation of King George VI, with Communist party activists closely watched before the Westminster Abbey ceremony in 1937. While the party prepared a propaganda drive and printed a million anti-monarchist leaflets to be distributed during coronation week, members were warned to avoid antagonising a largely pro-royalist public. One MI5 report from April 1937 noted that a “comrade” in Manchester had been “severely censured” for proposing a series of demonstrations, as it would be “playing into the hands of the fascists and police”. “It has been pointed out that members will be ‘going against the stream’ in doing this and they must be careful to speak in such a way that they do not make themselves unpopular with their neighbours.”

Sir Michael Tippett, a leading British composer of the 20th century and a famed pacifist, was also monitored by MI5 as a suspected Trotskyist revolutionary, according to the files. MI5 believed he joined first the Communist party and then the Trotskyists in the 1930s, and remained an active supporter until the end of the second world war.

The files suggest, however, that he was unconvincing as a revolutionary. In one intercepted letter to a Communist party organiser in London, he complained of the difficulties of trying to combine his work as a communist with his life as a music teacher living in rural Surrey; his evening commitments meant it was “quite impossible” for him to attend “cell” meetings in London. A report from 1955 noted that Tippett “has not come to notice in connection with communist or Trotskyist affairs”.

His radical past meant that, as late as 1959, he was blocked from taking up a Foreign Office-sponsored lectureship in Germany, and it was only in the 1960s that MI5 were prepared to give him a clean bill of health. In 1966 he was knighted for services to music; he died in 1998, aged 93.
output.standfirst: An MI5 officer who reviewed Aneurin Bevan's file after his death called it 'remarkably tame', despite the NHS founder being monitored for more than two decades over his links to communists and a Russian spy.
output.progress: Papers now released show nothing in Bevan's file to indicate MI5 ever tapped his phone or intercepted his mail.

output.headline: Met investigation opens, with specialist support for woman who came forward
output.bodyHtml:
Specialist officers are supporting a woman whose allegation that the former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson raped her inside parliament in 2016 is now being investigated by the Metropolitan police.

Scotland Yard confirmed it received a report from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) on 13 October about an alleged rape in the Palace of Westminster involving a man now aged 63. The woman has been interviewed by PSNI officers, who referred the case to the Met because the alleged offence was said to have taken place in London.

A Met spokesperson said: "On Tuesday 13 October, the Met received a report, referred to us by Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), relating to an allegation of rape in 2016, by a man now aged 63.

"The allegation relates to one victim who is being supported by specialist officers. The investigation is in its early stages. No arrests have been made and inquiries remain ongoing."

The Met confirmed that the alleged rape was reported to have taken place inside parliament in 2016.

The Belfast Telegraph first reported the allegation concerning a woman from Northern Ireland. The newspaper reported that Donaldson invited the woman on a tour of the Commons where he introduced her to high-profile figures. He was said to have taken her for dinner before bringing her into the DUP's offices in parliament.

The newspaper also reported that the woman received a photo of Donaldson during the Covid lockdown showing a filter on Snapchat across his face with a message saying: "Ready to face the world as soon as this isolation lark is over."

Donaldson was the leader of the DUP from 2021 to 2024.
output.standfirst: Specialist officers are supporting a woman after Scotland Yard opened an inquiry into an allegation that the former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson raped her in parliament in 2016, following a referral from the Police Service of Northern Ireland.
output.progress: Specialist officers continue to support the woman as the investigation proceeds; the Met says no arrests have been made and inquiries remain ongoing.

output.headline: Waitrose expands estate again with £1bn investment plan now under way
output.bodyHtml:
As part of a £1bn investment plan, Waitrose has chosen Cricklewood in north London as the location for its first supermarket in eight years.

The upmarket grocer will open the store on Thursday and another supermarket in Hale Barns, Greater Manchester, next month. It also plans four smaller stores next year, including a supermarket in Oakham, Rutland, and three convenience stores in Bedminster (Bristol), Chalk Farm (London) and Springstead Village (Cambridge).

In 2024, Waitrose, which has more than 300 supermarkets, said it planned to open up to four large supermarkets and 100 convenience stores over five years and would also refurbish a number of outlets introducing meat, fish and sushi counters, on-site bakeries and fine wine sections.

Tina Mitchell, the retail director at Waitrose, said: “Our supermarkets provide the ultimate showcase for everything that sets Waitrose apart – from our unmatched quality and industry-leading welfare standards to the expert service of our partners.”

This year the company – led since January by the former Tesco executive Tom Denyard - also plans to refurbish 29 stores.

On Wednesday, the John Lewis Partnership, which owns Waitrose and is itself owned by its staff, announced it had signed its first company-wide union recognition deal, ahead of new rights of union access in workplaces that come into force at the end of this month. Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of the shopworkers’ union Usdaw, said: “Usdaw already has members working within the business and this agreement will strengthen that presence and help us in supporting and representing members across the partnership. We now look forward to growing our membership and influence within the partnership and to working with the partnership’s management on finalising the details of how the agreement will work in practice.”

After a difficult period, when sales were hit by IT problems which led to gaps on shelves, Waitrose is holding market share, according to the latest figures from market analysts Worldpanel by Numerator, even as the chain comes under pressure from Marks & Spencer, which now has a higher share of the grocery market, under some measures, after opening a number of new food-led outlets.

Sales at Waitrose rose 4% in the six months to 1 August, though its underlying operating profit slid by £7m to £103m as it invested in keeping prices down and improving its loyalty scheme, and was also hit by higher energy costs during the summer heat wave.

The John Lewis Partnership reported a £98m pre-tax loss in the half-year to 1 August, as sales fell at the department stores despite heavy investment in updating the outlets. The company has been reducing the number of staff it employs directly as it tries to trim costs.
output.standfirst: The grocer's new Cricklewood store is the first of several openings under a £1bn investment plan, even as underlying profit slipped to £103m and parent John Lewis Partnership posted a £98m half-year loss.
output.progress: John Lewis Partnership has signed its first company-wide union recognition deal with Usdaw, ahead of new workplace access rights taking effect this month.

output.headline: Young Palestinians use stones to save US photojournalist from settler mob
output.bodyHtml:
The Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured by Israeli settlers in the West Bank on Friday has described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians.

Heidi Levine sustained four fractured vertebrae, two broken ribs and four puncture wounds when she was knocked to the ground and repeatedly beaten by a crowd of masked settlers while she and other journalists were covering the olive harvest in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah.

It is unclear whether the puncture wounds were caused by knives or other weapons. Levine said a witness to her attack had seen nails sticking out of some of the wooden clubs wielded by her attackers.

Levine, 64, has covered multiple wars and had just returned from an assignment in Ukraine before Friday’s attack. She said she would most likely have been killed had she not been wearing protective body armour and a helmet.

“I probably would have been dead, because for sure it doesn’t take much to kill a person with blows to the head,” she said shortly before being discharged from hospital on Wednesday in the Israeli city of Petah Tikva.

Levine pointed out that Palestinians did not have such protection and more than 20 had been killed in settler attacks so far this year, in the course of an escalating campaign of aggression – described as terrorism by Israeli security leaders – across the West Bank, aimed at driving Palestinians from their land.

“Every single journalist who looked at [the attack on me] are thinking they and I have gone to so many funerals of Palestinians killed by settlers,” Levine said.

She said the olive harvesting at Abu Falah had begun peacefully but at some point a group of young masked settlers appeared on a nearby hilltop watching the group of Palestinian villagers, journalists and human rights activists accompanying them. Levine said the attack began only after the Israeli army arrived on the scene.

“Then all hell broke loose. Some of the farmers started to gather their tarps and bags of olives that they had picked,” she said. “Then all of a sudden I hear a machine gun, and then saw teargas in the distance. I started to run … It was just like a lot of commotion and then all of a sudden I see a dozen of them and they started charging at me.

“I managed to keep my face to the ground, and I don’t know if I took that position to protect myself with my face down or it was their initial blow. Otherwise my whole face would have been broken and I could have suffered brain damage or lost an eye.

“They started kicking me and beating me with sticks. I can’t even count how many times, probably more than a hundred times. I actually tried playing dead so that they would stop. But it didn’t work.”

Witnesses said the beating only ceased when young Palestinian men used slingshots to aim stones at settlers forcing them back, allowing another American journalist, Jasper Nathaniel, to reach Levine and, with other reporters, help her to safety.

“The shabab [Palestinian youth] put themselves in front and were trying to keep them [the settlers] away, keep a protective shield, which was amazing. It was like a biblical battle,” Levine said.

After the attack, Nathaniel wrote: “Had the shabab not stepped up to protect her, she might well be dead. It is no exaggeration to say that young Palestinians armed only with stones risked their lives to save Heidi Levine’s.”

He said the army pursued the young Palestinians after the incident, rather than the settlers. Palestinians risk being shot by settlers or soldiers if they try to resist attacks, and can face long periods in detention without charge.

Levine, who has lived in Israel for four decades, said she would go back to reporting on the West Bank as soon as she recovered. “My work is important,” she said. “They have bruised me, broken some bones, but they haven’t cracked my spirit.”

Since the attack, she has received letters from Israelis expressing regret, and an apologetic phone call from the president, Isaac Herzog.

“He was a teddy bear on the phone,” she said. “He kept saying I just want to give you a big hug and these are not representative of who this country is, they’re a dark stain, and he called them thugs.”

The office of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, however, put out a statement on X seeking to cast doubt on witness and video accounts of what he called an “alleged attack”.

Levine was particularly angered by Netanyahu’s claim that some video footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual”.

“That’s such bullshit. They helped me up because they couldn’t get my things off of me. That’s why,” Levine said. “They robbed me of everything I have – a pouch with my documents, my American passport, credit card, camera disk and a small camera bag with two other lenses. Everything is gone … That’s why [they stood me up], and then they threw me back down and continued to kick and hit me.”

The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, called the attack a “despicable act of terror” and demanded prosecutions. Israeli police arrested 10 suspects after the Abu Falah incident and another attack on Saturday aimed at European diplomats near the West Bank village of Taybeh.

On Wednesday an Israeli court released four suspects in the attack on Levine and put them under house arrest, on the grounds there was insufficient evidence to keep them in custody.

Asked if she expected her attackers to be brought to justice, Levine said her level of confidence was “two out of 10”.

“I am not very hopeful,” she said. “Of course, if the government made the decision to do something and crack down on this and get people arrested, they would do it. But it’s not just arresting these teenage thugs. It’s going after their leaders, the rabbis, and how they’re organised.”
output.standfirst: Palestinian youths drove off masked settlers with stones to rescue Heidi Levine, who suffered fractured vertebrae, broken ribs and puncture wounds in the West Bank attack and criticised Netanyahu's response to it.
output.progress: Israeli police have arrested 10 suspects over the attack on Levine and a separate assault on diplomats near Taybeh, and Israel's president has apologised to Levine by phone, calling her attackers 'thugs'.

output.headline: 18 again: I returned to my life in 1983, to reckless adventures in a world soaked in alcohol
output.trail: Sundays were deadly, the generation gap between parents and their kids was enormous, and a pint cost 50p. The frisson of casual violence was everywhere. When I left school and set off to travel, I had no sense at all of where I was going.

output.headline: Nish Kankiwala appointed to lead turnaround at John Lewis and Waitrose
output.trail: The first group chief executive takes charge of the staff-owned partnership as it struggles to turn around a business hit by rising costs.

output.headline: Waitrose offers free coffees to boost police presence in stores
output.trail: The initiative comes as the retailer has seen a rise in theft and aggression.

output.headline: John Lewis strikes £500m deal with Abrdn to build 1,000 rental homes
output.trail: The partnership will redevelop Waitrose stores in Bromley and West Ealing, plus a vacant warehouse in Reading, to create new rental housing.

output.headline: What lies behind a difficult year for John Lewis and Waitrose
output.trail: Financial woes, the cost of living crisis and tougher competition are among the problems behind an expected second-ever full-year loss.

output.headline: Sharon White survives staff rebellion at John Lewis and Waitrose
output.trail: The boss of middle England's favourite retailer has weathered a staff rebellion, though she remains under pressure to rethink her strategy.

output.headline: Photojournalist Heidi Levine recovers as US ambassador seeks justice over attack
output.trail: Mike Huckabee has called the attack on Levine, 63, 'terror' and demanded the arrest and prosecution of those responsible, as she recovers in hospital in Israel.
output.progress: The US ambassador has called for the arrest and prosecution of those responsible for the attack.

output.headline: Six people killed in West Bank violence involving settlers and Israeli forces
output.trail: Four Palestinians and two Israelis died and several were hurt after armed settlers entered a village with military support; Israel is planning an 'extensive' military operation in response.

output.headline: Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine and Palestinian olive farmers hurt in settler attack
output.trail: Settlers threw rocks at Palestinian farmers and beat photographer Heidi Levine, in attacks that recur each year to disrupt the olive harvest.

output.headline: Palestinian boy, 14, and another killed in settler attack near West Bank school
output.trail: Local officials and witnesses say the attackers first shot at students, then at those who went to help them.

output.headline: Palestinians brace for further land seizures by Israeli settlers ahead of election
output.trail: A growing number of outposts are using violence to seize territory, a process seemingly enabled by radical elements in Netanyahu's government.

output.headline: Attack on Palestinian director highlights rising settler violence, activists say
output.trail: Activists say unprecedented levels of violence, with the apparent backing of Israeli authorities, are part of a drive to force Palestinians out of the West Bank.

output.headline: Basic income scheme helps protect Amazon rainforest in Peru, study finds
output.trail: Researchers found that almost 90% of participants in Peru's unconditional basic income pilot adopted environmentally beneficial practices, helping protect the rainforest.

output.headline: One-celled alga helps scientists win Nobel prize
output.trail: Chlamydomonas and its light-sensing protein helped researchers show how memories, feelings and behaviour form in the brain.

output.headline: Shedding weight in middle age can restore heart health, research suggests
output.trail: A UK study of 6,000 patients found that losing 5% of body weight may help cut the risk of stroke and heart disease.

output.headline: Archaeologist finally solves mystery of Westminster Abbey's Roman sarcophagus
output.trail: The skeleton inside the coffin, inscribed to Valerius Amandinus, is likely to be the remains of an 11th-century abbot, the archaeologist says.

output.headline: Budget boost puts Stratford International on track for cross-Channel trains
output.trail: Sadiq Khan says the upgrade would unlock the station's potential and let it live up to its name by becoming truly international.

output.headline: Hi-vis guardians keep nightly vigil over South Korea's canal shark
output.trail: Self-appointed guardians carrying selfie sticks watch over the shark that has been trapped in a South Korean canal for a month, a vigil that has drawn more than 1.6 million visitors.
output.progress: The nightly vigil has already drawn more than 1.6 million visitors to see the shark.

output.headline: Home Office drops bid to deport man after 50 years in UK
output.trail: The department has abandoned efforts to return Tony Hall, 62, to Barbados, a country he left at 12 and where he has no living relatives.
